## Report on Buckley et al., “The free energy principle for action and perception”

**1. The question, frozen.** The paper answers several. Its title and opening make the central one: *What is the mathematical structure of this predictive-coding implementation of the free energy principle, and what assumptions does it need?* Range: action, perception, learning; static and dynamic models; Gaussian beliefs. Asked: describe and derive, not test whether the FEP is true. I froze that.

**2. Jobs and parts.** Jobs, all given by the paper: upper-bound surprisal; approximate the Bayesian posterior; make the bound computable; derive prediction-error form; handle changing environments; include action; include learning; disclose assumptions. I added none.

Parts: R-density, G-density, informational free energy (IFE), KL link, Laplace/Gaussian assumption, neural encoding of sufficient statistics, sharp-peak/Taylor expansion, prediction errors, variances/precisions, generative model, prior, generalised coordinates, gradient descent on brain state, action as control, learning the G-density, survival constraint, biological plausibility.

**3. Part by part.**

| Part | Mark | Why |
|---|---|---|
| R-density \(q(\vartheta)\) | **held** | Remove: no IFE, no approximate posterior. Its Gaussian form is a separate part below. |
| G-density \(p(\vartheta,\phi)=p(\phi|\vartheta)p(\vartheta)\) | **held** | Needed to compute IFE without the true posterior. |
| IFE \(F=\int q\ln(q/p)\) | **held** | Remove: no upper bound, no variational objective. |
| KL link \(F+\ln p(\phi)=D_{KL}\) | **held** | Remove: no reason minimising \(F\) improves the posterior. |
| Laplace/Gaussian R-density | **fixed** | The owner sets it for tractability. Paper says ensemble learning is another route, not tested here. |
| Neural variables encode sufficient statistics | **borrowed** | Rests on predictive coding/neural coding, not tested here. |
| Sharp-peak/Taylor expansion | **fixed** | A simplification. Paper itself flags non-trivial implications. |
| Prediction errors \(\varepsilon_z,\varepsilon_w\) | **held** | Remove: no quadratic energy, no predictive-coding form. |
| Variances/precisions | **held if** | Held by confidence-weighting job; actual values unknown or learned. |
| Generative model \(\phi=g(\mu;\theta)+z\) | **fixed** | Chosen form; Gaussian noise assumed. Swap noise law: prediction-error form changes. |
| Prior \(\mu=\bar\mu+w\) | **fixed** | Chosen; encodes expectations. |
| Generalised coordinates | **held** | Remove: static model only; loses changing environments. |
| Gradient descent on \(\mu\) | **held** | Remove: no mechanism for minimising IFE by perception. |
| Action as control via inverse model | **held if** | Held by control interpretation. Rival role — experimentation — is noted but left out. |
| Learning the G-density | **borrowed** | Rests on hierarchical predictive coding/deep learning; not tested. |
| Survival constraints conducive to survival | **borrowed** | Rests on evolutionary/homeostatic theory; not tested. |
| Biological plausibility | **unknown** | No neural test here. Would need a measurable neural prediction. |
| IFE vs prediction-error form | **two routes** | Under Gaussian/Laplace, both minimise the same thing. Either alone would do. |

**4. Whole-explanation checks.**  
*Flip.* If an organism increased surprisal, the FEP would call it non-viable. Without a gauge, that is a catch-all. The simple agent model gives specific trajectories, so some pokes exist. But the general principle can absorb many behaviours by changing expectations.  
*Direction.* Most of the paper runs forward from assumptions to equations. The action part risks running backward: it starts from a desired trajectory and assumes a suitable inverse model. That answers “what can be told” more than “what produces action.”  
*Answer hidden in starting points.* “Viable/autopoietic organisms must resist disorder” carries the normative force. The maths derives prediction errors once that plus Gaussian assumptions are in. It does not derive *why* minimise IFE except from survival.  
*Add a job.* Ask for a case where FEP and a rival objective predict different behaviour. Under Gaussian assumptions, FEP, variational Bayes and predictive coding are the same at this level. No listed change separates them. The paper notes this.  
*Pull.* Precision weighting pulls against prediction errors: high precision makes errors dominate; low precision makes the prior dominate. Action as control pulls against action as experimentation: one satisfies expectations, the other seeks information. Model complexity pulls against tractability. These lines are drawn by assumptions, not tests.  
*Catch-alls.* “Viable”, “homeostatic/autopoietic” are broad. A gauge would be a measured loss of homeostasis. That is post hoc unless measured before. The paper does disclose many assumptions, which helps.  
*Change list.* Covered: sensory input, environmental dynamics, noise variances, model parameters, action, learning, static/dynamic. Left out: non-Gaussian posteriors/noise, non-homeostatic agents, multiple agents, action as experimentation, embodiment, neural implementation details. Some are stated openly.  
*Rivals.* Bayesian brain, predictive coding, optimal control. No change on the list separates FEP from predictive coding on the derived equations. A finer question is needed.  
*Provenance.* Many parts are borrowed from variational Bayes, statistical physics and predictive coding. The derivations and simple agent model are built. The simple model’s choices are not clearly fitted or tested.

**5. What would make it harder to vary.** Tie one prediction to a neural or behavioural measurement that would fail if IFE were not minimised. Replace the survival catch-all with a measurable gauge. Test action-as-control against action-as-experimentation. Derive the non-Gaussian case.

**6. What this does not show.** Hard to vary is not truth. The paper is a mathematical review, not a test of the FEP against brain data.

**7. One next step.** Run a poke on the paper’s simple agent: compare FEP action-as-control against an experimentation agent on a task where expected sensory input and information gain pull apart. See which part moves.
